subject: monsterTruck
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: monster truck with huge tyres.
Style: pixel art.
reasoning:
I need to plan a monster truck build in pixel art style, going through the vehicle builder with exactly one root joint for the chassis, plus separate wheel joints to allow spinning.

For dimensions, I'm working out realistic monster-truck proportions: tyre radius around 0.85m, overall length near 4.5m, with the body sitting high above the axles. I'm figuring out how to construct textured tyres using the pixel kit's cell-paint tools to create a blocky tread pattern on a cylinder geometry oriented along the axle.

Still writing tyre paint logic...

Actually, I'm thinking I should split the wheel into separate parts: the tyre cylinder with tread, plus a rim disc protruding slightly, with a textured hub face using a pixelated circle texture showing lug bolts, oriented outward to face the viewer.

I'll add a dashed white lettering ring to the tyre sidewall for that painted-tyre look. For the wheel, I'm orienting the cylinder along the x-axis with 16 radial segments so the tread cell-paint logic can select between y/z axes based on normal direction, giving a jagged pixel-art pattern around the rim.

For the tyre tread itself, I'm thinking of actually modeling chunky lugs as merged box geometries placed around the circumference in two staggered rows offset across the tyre width, rather than relying purely on texture.

Working out wheel radius with lugs included — base tyre at 0.80, lugs extending to about 0.88 — so I need to make sure the lowest contact point still rests properly at floor level given that lugs rotate around and a gap might be at the very bottom rather than a lug tip.

I'm figuring the centre y should sit around 0.87, accounting for lugs staggered across two rows at 14 positions so one row's flat face lands at the bottom. That keeps sink well under the 2% tolerance, with total model height around 3.4. Now I'm setting up the lug geometry as a group of box shapes.

Merging lug box geometries...

I'm setting up a part-helper function for building box geometry pieces attached to the body bone, then planning the paint scheme — a bright red-orange body with flame decals and a bold name like "CRUSHER" rendered using a tiny pixel font I'll need to hand-draw letter by letter.

Now I'm designing the chassis: steel rails, cross members, front and rear axles, differential housings, and suspension link bars for the monster truck frame.

Shocks should angle from axle up to frame, colored in a yellow metal tone. Now I'm working out the proper ride height: axle around y=0.88, frame around y=1.45, with tyres topping out near 1.76 so the body floor should sit near 1.7 and the roof around 3.0 to get that proper monster truck stance.

I'm setting the body floor at y=1.75, cab around 3.15 tall, with the chassis peeking through between the tyres like a real fibreglass-bodied truck. For track width, I'm placing tyre centers at x=±1.45 with 0.6 width tyres, so the body at ±0.95 width clears the inner tyre edges nicely. For wheelbase, axles sit at z=±1.3 giving tyre extents to ±2.18, with the body running roughly 4.6m overall including bumpers, and now I'm blocking out the body silhouette piece by piece starting with the hood section.

Now I'm defining the lower tub (full-length base box), hood with a raised intake scoop, and the cab box with a tapered roof and windshield slope — building the truck's main body volumes in stacked boxes.

Defining the cab outline points...

Calculating the windshield plane's normal direction and placement, sizing it to fit the slope, and planning a glass texture with diagonal highlights for it.

Now moving to the side windows, I'm figuring out trapezoid-shaped planes facing ±x, sizing a pixel texture so the transparent region matches the trapezoid outline, and working out the plane's local axes for proper orientation against the car body.

For -X side the front ends up on the right, which means the window texture needs to be mirrored for that side to keep the text reading correctly from outside. Rather than using negative scaling (which flips winding), I'll make two versions of the texture or draw with a mirror flag depending on which side is being rendered.

I'm settling on roughly 10 textures total: glass, side windows (left/right), hub, grille/headlight, flame decals (mirrored per side), lettering/number signage, license plate or logo, hood scoop, and tire sidewall paint. I'm planning decal placement as flat planes on the tub's vertical sides, positioned to avoid overlapping the wheel arches since the tub sits narrower than the wheel track.

Now I'm defining a pixel-style body paint function using a red color ramp with dithering, where brightness depends on the surface normal — brighter on top faces, mid-tone on sides, darker at the front — plus a touch of random noise for texture.

I'm also planning to darken the lower body with height, confirming cellPaint works fine on extrusions and boxes, and settling on a retro arcade color scheme — leaning toward a bright cyan-blue body with yellow-orange flame accents and a big spring suspension for that classic pixel monster-truck vibe.

Now I'm working out the blue color ramp, chrome/yellow rims, and a flame decal texture — sketching a sawtooth-based tongue profile that rises from the front-bottom and licks toward the back, shading from yellow to deeper tones by height.

Adding the mirrored flame texture now. For sponsor lettering like "CRUSHER," I'm deciding where it fits best—maybe a banner on the roof as a sun-visor sign rather than crowding the flame-covered tub side, since the cab side is mostly window.

I'll use a finer texel for decals, 0.05 instead of the main 0.1, since detail work needs half or a third the resolution. With a 3x5 font at that scale, seven letters come out to about 1.35m wide and 0.25m tall, which fits reasonably against the cab's 1.55m length for the side lettering plane positioned on the lower cab band.

Now I'm laying out the body more precisely to avoid overlap: a tub spanning roughly ±0.95m wide and 1.75-2.35m up, with a shorter front to leave room for a grille; a hood sitting above that from 2.35-2.6m with a scoop rising to 2.8m; and I want to add a chrome supercharger blower sticking out of the hood like a classic monster truck, with intake stacks and a chrome top.

I'm continuing to plan the cab (extruded above the hood line, 1.8m wide), the truck bed behind it with walls, tailgate, and floor plus a rollbar, and deciding to skip traditional fenders since monster truck tires sit outside the body -- now moving on to the front bumper design.

Working out bumper, grille, and headlight placement...

Rather than making the whole grille texture emissive, I should add separate glowing headlight boxes (yellowish-white, roughly 0.35x0.25x0.08) positioned at either side of the front, with the grille texture plane between them having dark sockets where the lights sit, offset slightly to avoid z-fighting.

Now I'm planning more exterior details: roof-mounted light cubes with glow plus a visor, chrome exhaust stacks rising behind the cab with glowing orange flame tips, a chrome roll cage arch over the bed, and rear elements like a bumper, glowing red tail lights, and a license plate texture.

For realism I'm adding mud splatter to the lower body and tires using noise-based paint thresholds, plus full chassis detail—frame rails, crossmembers, driveshaft, differentials, axle tubes, 4-link bars, yellow-sprung shocks, and steering links—along with wheel joints, lug nuts, hubs, painted sidewalls, and beadlock bolts.

Now I'm thinking about the base/setting: a classic monster truck pose standing over crushed cars on a dirt arena platform, maybe with a ramp. The tricky part is that a dirt base platform would sit below y=0 while the tires need to touch y=0, which conflicts with the rule that nothing should extend below the floor—I need to figure out how to stage this without violating that constraint.

I'm weighing how to apply the ground offset consistently—maybe a helper that shifts every y-coordinate, or a global constant added at the point level, though that's risky for lathe shapes and paths. I'm also considering whether the base slab could sit flush rather than underground to avoid this complication entirely.

I'm thinking of placing crushed cars as props near the truck's front to add storytelling detail, maybe a small stack of two, though that risks making the composition lopsided. I'm sketching out the base footprint dimensions to keep the truck filling the frame while leaving room ahead for the dirt ramp and wreck props.

Now I'm working through sizing the dirt slab base relative to the truck's tires and figuring out where a crushed car prop could fit without extending the base too wide, considering tires stacked at back-right, a checkered flag pole at rear-left, and scattered traffic cones for atmosphere.

I'll also add a stack of small tyres, cones, and a checkered flag post at the rear for scene detail, plus stepped dirt mounds. The overall model stays around length 7.9 by width 6 with truck height 3.4, and I'm building the crushed car from flattened body and cabin boxes with a dark window texture and flattened wheel cylinders, painted with a rusty finish.

Now I'm sizing out the crushed car pieces further—a tilted cabin box, thin dark window strips, and squashed cylinder wheels—plus scattering small details like bolts, rivets, and dirt pebbles as merged parts to push the total part count into the 150-200 range while keeping quality high.

Setting up imports from the agentic-3js-builder module and its pixel/glow/clockwork kits, planning to keep the import list minimal to just what I actually need like createBuilder, rng, noise, and the curve helpers.

Defining color palettes...

Now I'm adding tire colors and writing the body paint function that layers mud splatter near the lower part of the tub based on height and noise, with mud kicking in below roughly y=1.78.

I'm also setting up a brightness value combining vertical and lateral normal components to fake a front-top-left light source, adding slight random and noise variation, and darkening the lower areas for grime. This paint function applies consistently across the cab's extruded surfaces too, so the coloring stays continuous across hood and body panels.

For decorative trim, I'm considering a racing stripe but the hood's blower housing blocks the usual centerline placement, so I'm skipping hood/roof stripes and instead thinking about a trim stripe along the tub's top edge on the side faces, though that area overlaps with the flame decal plane, so I'll likely skip that too and move on to the front details.

For the chassis I'm defining a dark steel paint function that picks a steel color based on surface normal and position with a dithered texture, then setting up a chrome paint with lighter banded coloring for shiny parts like the stacks, using sine-based value bands tied to normal direction to simulate reflective highlights on cylindrical surfaces.

For the springs I'm using a flat yellow color, and for the tires I'm defining a paint function based on distance from the wheel center to create concentric rings -- a darker rubber band near the rim edge, and I'm working out a dashed white ring further out using angle calculations around the wheel to simulate tread lettering or sidewall markings.

Still writing tire paint logic...

For the cylinder caps along the x-axis, I'm making sure the sidewall covers the full disc while the hub fills its inner portion.

Now I'm sizing the tire geometry with lugs extending its outer radius, and planning the hub disc texture as a pixel grid where distance from center determines rings and bolt placement.

Still writing hub texture code...

Now setting up the wheel joint naming convention, using FL/FR/BL/BR for front-left, front-right, back-left, back-right, with the left side pointing in the +X direction and right side -X for the joint axes.

I'm pinning down the actual dimensions: tyre radius, chassis width, front and rear wheelbase positions, and confirming the body length places rear tyres slightly beyond the rear bumper, which should look fine visually.

I'm also planning the joint hierarchy — a root chassis joint plus four wheel joints — and considering whether to add an optional hood hinge joint for extra detail, positioning its pivot near the rear edge of the hood with an appropriate hinge axis direction.

Writing helper functions for part placement...

I'll keep the bed simple with a floor, walls, roll bar, and two cargo crates reusing the planks texture to save effort. Now I'm planning the texture list: glass windshield, left/right side windows, hub, flame decals, grille, and side lettering spelling "CRUSH."

I'm working out the mirroring logic so "CRUSHER" reads correctly on both sides without needing separate textures, then adding planks, a reused banner texture for the windshield visor, a checker flag, and deciding whether to include a license plate or just a number decal on the door.

For the plate, I'm scoping out a minimal 3x5 pixel font covering just the letters needed for "CRUSH" plus "4X4", simplifying by skipping a full alphabet and instead putting a short "4X4" decal on the tailgate.

Defining pixel font glyphs and text rendering...

I'm sizing the "CRUSHER" text texture so its plane fits within the cab's side band, computing width/height from glyph count and padding, and checking it aligns with the window boundary and flat cab side position.

Now I'm mapping out the cab outline coordinates in absolute space, tracing how the windshield's slanted A-pillar connects down to the lower cab corners and verifying the window region sits correctly against the cab's front and side geometry.

Still computing window geometry and texture mapping coordinates...

Still computing glass texture and placement...

Now I'm thinking about adding a sun visor above the windshield — a thin flat box spanning the roof width, sitting at the top of the cab around y 3.2-3.26, positioned to project slightly forward without tilting, keeping it simple and aligned with the cab's flat roof.

Adjusting the visor height so it clears the windshield top without hiding it, then sizing the name banner plane to fit within the visor's front face.

I'm placing four roof lights atop the visor, spaced evenly and glowing white-yellow, then positioning the front grille plane on the tub at the right height to sit centered against the cab.

For the grille texture itself, I'm drawing a dark background with recessed headlight sockets at both ends, horizontal chrome slats alternating with dark gaps across the middle, and considering a small centered emblem before adding glowing headlight overlays on top.

Now I'm placing the chrome front bumper box beneath the grille, then adding a bull bar structure with vertical tubes and a top cross brace in front of it for detail.

I'll use square tube rods (4-sided) for a pixelated chrome look, skip tow hooks and license plate details, and move on to roughing out the bed floor dimensions.

For the bed, I'm placing the floor plank slab on top of the tub box, then adding side walls (0.1 thick, 0.4 tall) running from the cab back to near the tailgate, painted in body color, followed by a tailgate panel closing off the rear.

Now I'm positioning the license plate decal and tail light boxes onto the tailgate's rear face, working out the exact z-offsets so they sit flush and don't clip through, then checking the texture orientation math for a plane facing backward so the decal isn't mirrored.

I'm also planning the rear bumper as a chrome box and sketching a roll bar structure in the bed using an arch of tube segments defined by polyline sweeps.

Now I'm positioning dual exhaust stacks behind the cab, aligning their radius and height so they sit flush against the cab's back face near the roll bar.

Adding flame tips, collar rings, and planning the hood geometry with bolt details and a blower box on top.

Adding chrome injector stacks around the scoop top, then moving to the chassis layer underneath the body — steel rails along the sides and cross members spaced along the length to tie the frame together.

For the body mounts I'm placing small blocks bridging the gap between rails and tub, then working out the axle assembly: housings spanning the width, with planetary hub covers at the wheel ends in a brass gold finish to sit flush with the tyres.

I'm shaping the differential pumpkin as a scaled sphere with a bolted cover plate in steel, then running a driveshaft rod connecting the front and rear differentials along the centerline.

Now I'm working out the suspension four-link geometry, placing upper and lower link rods between each axle and the frame for both front and rear axles, keeping the angles steep to match a monster-truck style setup.

I'm also positioning the coilover shocks for each wheel, checking their length and placement so they sit visibly between the tire and tub without clipping through the body panels.

Sweeping the coil paths onto the chassis with chrome spring shading, then adding a tie rod across the front axle for steering links. I'm skipping extras like hydraulic rams and skid plates for now, and planning a dirt base slab beneath the truck.

Working out the slab dimensions and position so tyre lugs sit just into the surface without clipping, then checking the bounding box against the full model height for scale. Now I'm setting up the dirt texture with noise, dithering, and tyre track grooves pressed into the surface.

Now I'm adding dirt mounds at the corners as stacked pyramid layers, and sizing a crushed car placed near the truck's bumper, scaling it down from real car proportions so it fits the scene as a shortened, toy-like crushed wreck.

Positioning the crushed car at z center 3.9 with a slight rotation, then working out its body, cabin, windows, and crumpled hood/trunk as separate angled boxes since I can't use a group transform and need to compute each rotated offset manually.

Planning the junkyard details now: stacked tires with tread paint, a cone on top, and a few traffic cones using simple pyramid cone geometry with orange paint and a white band.

For the flag, I'm placing a chrome pole with a checker-textured flag made from a thin box since it's simpler than wrestling with card orientation for a flat plane.

Let me finalize the checker pattern at 6x4 squares for the flag, then add a pole topper ball, side mirrors with stalks near the cab front, and skip extra decals like door seams or sponsor logos to keep things simple. I'll also check wheel arch clearance, making sure the tires sit with enough gap inside the tub edges.

Skipping mud flaps, underglow, and wipers to keep it clean. I'm adding a roof antenna rod and placing flame decal planes on the tub sides, sizing the texture and positioning them within the tub's height so they don't overlap the bed walls or lettering.

Designing flame texture pattern...

Computing flame height from the profile curve, then coloring pixels by vertical position—yellow core near bottom, orange mid, red toward the tip—with a dark outline row on top to make the flame pop against the blue background.

Now I'm designing the grille and plate textures: a small pixel grid spelling "4X4" in dark glyphs on a cream background with a bordered frame, then sizing the plate plane to fit proportionally on the rear tailgate.

I'm also planning a text-stamping helper to render glyphs onto textures, defining hub, window, and flame textures, and tallying up the total texture count to stay within an atlas budget—counting roughly 11 distinct pixel textures while keeping them deliberately low-res for a chunky, unsmoothed look.

Now I'm calculating paint texel density: estimating total painted surface area across tires, slab, and body (around 150 square meters), then working out that a 1024px paint sheet gives roughly 70 texels per meter, which checks out against the minimum "several texels wide" guidance for cell sizes—though I'm considering bumping up to a 2048px paint sheet just to be safe.

I'm weighing whether to shrink the painted surface area instead, since the slab's hidden bottom face likely counts toward paint area too, doubling it unnecessarily; separating the slab into distinct top/bottom geometry could help, but I'll just accept the larger paintSize for now and move on to picking a color-snapping helper function.

Now I'm sorting out the rng signature -- confirming it returns a callable function rather than an object with methods, since the kit docs suggest `rand?: () => number` -- so I'll call it like `r()` when scattering pebbles randomly across the slab.

I plan to merge the pebble boxes after translating and rotating them, applying flat stone-grey colors in light and dark shades since paint works fine on flat colors even without UVs. Setting up helper types and constants now before writing the full geometry code...

Next I need a pixel font system: a bitmap font map for characters, a function to convert text into pixel coordinates by walking each glyph and offsetting by character width, and a text-width calculator assuming each glyph is 3px wide with 1px spacing, used to size the name texture.

For "CRUSHER" I'm building a texture that stamps outline pixels first in dark navy, then overlays white foreground pixels on top, possibly adding a yellow drop-shadow layer for contrast against the blue cab body.

Now I'm designing the PLATE texture: a dark border fill with a cream interior rectangle, then stamping "4X4" text in blue across specific rows and columns using a fill function that takes coordinates and returns color. Next I'm starting on a PLANKS tile texture at 16x12 size with four plank divisions.

For the planks, I'm defining a fill function that marks every fourth row as a dark seam line and otherwise picks a wood shade from a palette using a deterministic hash based on x, y, and row position so the pattern looks varied but reproducible.

I'm also sketching a small checkered tile pattern and then building a glass windshield texture: a bordered frame with a vertical gradient that goes from a lighter blue near the top to darker toward the bottom, picking colors from a blue palette to simulate sky reflection and depth, plus some diagonal glint detailing.

Now I'm designing a wheel hub texture using radial distance from center to create concentric chrome rings and a lip highlight based on angle.

Adding darker beadlock bolt shading, then moving to design the tapering side window shape for the cab, narrower at the bottom than the top.

Writing flame rendering logic...

Now I'm designing the grille texture with headlight socket frames and chrome slat patterns, plus a center emblem.

Next I'm setting up the body paint logic, defining a mud line threshold based on noise so dirt gets applied near the lower body based on height.

Writing chrome shading logic...

Writing geometry helpers...

Writing wheel placement loop...

Shaping a tyre profile with a tread band and slightly wider sidewall cylinders to get that stepped, pixelated tire look.

I'm handling shoulder face coloring based on distance thresholds, then starting to build the lug geometry with boxes arranged in two offset rows around the tire circumference.

Still working through the lug positioning math...

For the bottom lug at row 0, i=0, the center position sits just above the flat bottom face at y=-0.88, giving a center y of about 0.87, which checks out. For lug coloring I'll reuse the same tyre paint function applied at the lug's local center position, since it reads model-space coordinates correctly and gives consistent mud/tire shading across both the tread and lugs.

Now I'm adding the hub detail: a white circle geometry mapped with the hub texture, positioned slightly forward on the wheel's axis, plus a small chrome center cap and a raised lip ring just behind it to give the hub some dimensionality.

I need to nudge the circle's offset slightly further out to avoid z-fighting with the sidewall cap cylinder. Now I'm setting up the suspension: importing a coil geometry for the springs, and planning shock placement — each wheel gets shocks running from the frame rails at x=±0.55 down to the axle at x=±0.85.

Working out shock dimensions...

Still working out link geometry...

Adding differential assembly...

Now I'm thinking through the driveshaft connecting the axles with U-joints, plus tie rods for four-wheel steering, and whether to add frame rails, chassis mounts, and a hidden fuel cell between the rails that peeks out between the tires.

I'm adding the fuel cell in red and a battery box under the tub, then sizing the tub itself, planning bumpers, and setting up a hood hinge joint. I'm also placing side mirrors with support stalks on each side of the cab.

Now I'm deciding the mirror color should be chrome, then thinking through door handle placement—realizing it would overlap the NAME text area, so I'm skipping handles and door seams. I'm also planning a roof vent and starting to position a rear antenna rod.

Antenna height gets bumped to 3.9-3.95 with a small orange tip, plus a tiny flag pennant, and I'm rechecking total model height stays reasonable.

Writing cab extrusion coordinates...

That hood overlap hides the cab front face at z=0.6, which works out fine. Now I'm working out the rear window glass plane dimensions and position, matching the texture's aspect ratio and placing it centered on the rear slope around y=2.75.

Next I'm positioning the exhaust stacks beside the rear window and roll bar, then adding the blower assembly on the hood—a steel housing box, a chrome scoop on top, and a dark intake opening, all layered along the hood's y-range.

Adding more lighting elements... headlights with warm glow, red taillights, orange exhaust flames, and amber roof lights, with chrome hood pins and bumper details.

Now I'm fleshing out the base scene elements—slab, mounds, crushed car, tyre stack, cones, flag, pebbles, grass tufts—and setting up a coordinate helper to rotate the crushed car's local points by its yaw angle around a chosen origin point.

Writing car geometry and paint...

Adding wheel cylinders with chrome hubs, bent bumper rods, a crushed plate, and small broken headlight glow details, then checking the vertical layering of the car so hood crumple sits correctly above the body. Now I'm sketching out a stepped mound function for the terrain piles.

Placing dirt mounds at a few coordinates, then building a tire stack from stacked cylinders with slight yaw offsets and a dark top disc to fake the hole.

Now I'm positioning a few scattered cones near the back of the lot, then scattering dozens of tiny pebble boxes randomly across the slab while avoiding the truck's footprint area.

I'm also adding small grass tufts along the slab edges for extra texture, and writing a helper function to merge all these box geometries together into a single mesh.

Then I'm setting up tyre sidewall detail painting, computing distance from a center point per cell to create a radial pattern...

Still writing tire pattern logic...

I'm sorting out priority order so mud overrides apply first, then checking caps and tread normals for the wheel geometry before starting on the final TypeScript module with mesh merging utilities.

Writing imports and constants...

I'm defining the pixel-glyph font set for the truck's lettering and the color palettes for the windows, then moving into the main build function.

Working out the shock absorber loop geometry, computing lower and upper mounting points along the axle and checking for clearance conflicts with the tub's underside.
